article_title: Federal Prosecutors Charge Atlanta Man for Wiping His Phone With a GrapheneOS 'Duress Password' at the Airport
summary: REJECTED as duplicate coverage: PR #2051, covering the same Sam Tunick / GrapheneOS duress-password prosecution, merged at 2026-07-27T12:52:35Z (merge commit 685c6dbb9) while this review was in progress. On its own editorial merits this submission would have been APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS (see editor_notes), but per newsroom duplicate-coverage policy only one article on a given story may publish, and #2051 has chronological priority and is now the published article. This submission is rejected as redundant, not for any quality defect.

findings.message: Quote misattributed to the wrong outlet
findings.details: The article states: 'Marlon Kautz, a member of the Atlanta Solidarity Fund, defended the use of privacy tools like GrapheneOS, telling [The Verge]: "We all have a right to secure our private data against unconstitutional searches..."' The Verge's own snapshot text reads: 'Marlon Kautz... told The Guardian earlier this week that, "we all have a right to secure our private data..."' -- i.e. The Verge itself credits the quote to The Guardian, not to a statement made to The Verge. The quote is accurate and verbatim in both snapshots, but the article cites the wrong outlet as the one Kautz spoke to.

findings.message: Detail attributed to 'the motion' that the source actually attributes to courtroom testimony
findings.details: The article states: 'The motion also states that Tunick "asked four times during the interrogation to speak with a lawyer, but was rebuffed each time," and that agents produced no warrant and did not read him his rights, according to [The Guardian].' The Guardian snapshot instead reads: 'Tunick asked four times during the interrogation to speak with a lawyer, but was rebuffed each time, according to courtroom testimony.' -- the Guardian attributes this specific detail to courtroom testimony at Monday's hearing, not to the text of the suppression motion itself. The underlying fact and quote are accurate and correctly cited to The Guardian overall; only the 'the motion states' framing is incorrect.

findings.message: Duplicate coverage: PR #2051 on the same story merged and published during this review
findings.details: PR #2051 ('US Charges Atlanta Activist for Using GrapheneOS Duress Password to Wipe Phone at Border') covers the identical underlying news event (Sam Tunick's federal prosecution over a GrapheneOS duress-password phone wipe at Hartsfield-Jackson airport) using largely the same two sources (The Verge, The Guardian). #2051 was opened before this PR (#2053), received its own Chief Editor review (verdict APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS, commit 84ddb80e0), and merged at 2026-07-27T12:52:35Z (merge commit 685c6dbb9), publishing the article. A third independent submission, PR #2054, also covers this story and remains open/unaffected by this decision. Per newsroom duplicate-coverage policy, only the first-merged article on a story is published; this submission is therefore rejected as redundant regardless of its own quality.

content_preview.title: Federal Prosecutors Charge Atlanta Man for Wiping His Phone With a GrapheneOS 'Duress Password' at the Airport
content_preview.summary: US prosecutors are pursuing an Atlanta man under a rarely used federal statute after he allegedly used a GrapheneOS 'duress password' to wipe his phone during a border search.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Federal prosecutors are charging Atlanta resident Sam Tunick under a little-known statute that makes it a crime to destroy property to prevent its seizure, after agents say he wiped his phone during a search at the airport, according to [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/policy/971097/us-charging-american-citizen-wiping-phone-duress-password) and [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/23/cop-city-protester-phone). Tunick was stopped at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlan...

recommendations: No rewrite or resubmission is invited for this specific submission -- under the v3.9.0 workflow REJECT discards the work, and in this case the topic itself is now covered by the published article from PR #2051.

Editorial/attribution issues noted below (Kautz quote misattributed to the wrong outlet; a courtroom-testimony detail misattributed to 'the motion') are recorded for the record even though this submission is not publishing, in case they are useful context if PR #2051's own corrections are later reviewed.

Process recommendation: when multiple bot runs pick up the same wire story independently, an earlier duplicate-detection pass before Chief Editor review would save reviewer time; this is not the first time convergent submissions on one story have required a duplicate-coverage rejection (see also the REJECT of a submission duplicating PR #2042's Hermes AI agent Thailand-breach coverage).

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News-category piece (597 words, within the 400-1200 range) with clear Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know sections. Neutral, professional tone; presents both the prosecution's destruction-of-evidence framing and the defense's unlawful-search framing; no AI self-reference; no sensationalism.
editor_notes.source_verification: Both sources were read in full from disk snapshots at sources/2026-07/federal-prosecutors-charge-atlanta-man-for-wiping-his-phone-with-a-grapheneos-duress-password-at-the-airport/, decompressed with gunzip, converted to plain text, and manually read end to end (not just keyword-grepped). Integrity independently verified: recomputed sha256 of each decompressed file matches manifest.json exactly before reading -- source-0.html.gz (The Verge, sha256 6577ebb0...5756d208, HTTP 200, no archive fallback) and source-1.html.gz (The Guardian, sha256 20658986...8d91d59ed, HTTP 200, no archive fallback). No live WebFetch was needed; both snapshots captured genuine article content (verified by reading the visible headline, byline, and body text, not an interstitial/captcha page). (1) source-0.html.gz (The Verge, byline Terrence O'Brien, dated Jul 26, 2026) -- confirms: DOJ prosecuting Sam Tunick; duress password wiped the phone when agents tried to seize it at Hartsfield-Jackson airport on January 24, 2025; a little-known, rarely-used statute criminalizing destruction of property to prevent seizure; GrapheneOS described as 'the privacy-focused GrapheneOS'; defense motion calls the stop 'a pretext for a fishing expedition into Mr Tunick's connections' to Stop Cop City; defense argues detention/seizure were unlawful; government countered a warrant wasn't required because Tunick had not yet been granted entry to the US (this government rebuttal is NOT included in the submitted article -- see recommendations); and, critically, the Kautz quote is explicitly attributed by The Verge itself to a statement made 'to The Guardian earlier this week' -- confirming the submitted article's attribution of this quote to The Verge is incorrect (finding above). (2) source-1.html.gz (The Guardian, byline Timothy Pratt, dated Thu 23 Jul 2026) -- confirms nearly every remaining specific in the article verbatim: the $109m Cop City training center and 'wide range of local and national organizations and protesters' opposing it; Tunick's placement on a terrorism watchlist unbeknownst to him; the secondary-inspection room with 'a table, several chairs and a camera and microphone'; interrogation questions centered on child sexual abuse images; the exact quoted phrase 'the screen went blank, flashed several times and the phone appeared to restart' (attributed by the Guardian to the motion); the exact quoted phrase 'a pretext for a fishing expedition into Mr Tunick's connections' (attributed to the motion); Christophe Boutry's exact quotes 'It's concerning – and sends the message that [GrapheneOS] is criminal by default,' 'main goal [of the operating system] is protection of privacy,' and 'They're our phones and the state can't tell us how to use them'; Boutry's title 'a cybersecurity and surveillance expert'; the Monday first hearing and end-of-October timeline for the suppression ruling; and the GrapheneOS description 'an open-source operating system that enables users to enter a passcode and wipe a phone clean.' However, the Guardian attributes the 'asked four times... rebuffed each time' detail to 'courtroom testimony,' not to the motion document as the submitted article states (finding above). Also NOT reflected in the submitted article: the CBP officer's (Larry Findley) on-record characterization of the stop as a routine search 'looking for anything that's prohibited,' and Boutry's additional remarks about similar GrapheneOS profiling patterns in France, Spain, and Catalonia -- omissions that affect completeness/balance but are not factual errors.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Two misattributions found, both subordinate specifics in the body (not in the headline, summary, or lead paragraph): (1) the Kautz quote is credited to The Verge when The Verge's own snapshot text attributes it to a statement made to The Guardian; (2) the lawyer-access/no-warrant detail is credited to 'the motion' when The Guardian's snapshot attributes it to courtroom testimony at the hearing on the motion. In both cases the quoted material itself is accurate and verbatim, and the underlying fact is true and properly traceable to a cited, verified source -- only the specific attribution mechanism/outlet is wrong. Every other quote, date, dollar figure, and named individual was checked against the relevant snapshot and confirmed accurate, including the January 24, 2025 date, the Dominican Republic vacation detail, the $109 million training-center figure, and all four Boutry/Kautz quotes' exact wording. No fabricated facts, no hallucinated quotes, no orphan body URLs (both cited URLs appear in article.sources).
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. Presents the prosecution's framing (destruction of evidence) and the defense's framing (unlawful search) side by side without editorializing. No AI self-reference.

editor_notes.duplicate_coverage_investigation: Per explicit editorial instruction, before finalizing any verdict I checked whether this PR duplicates other in-flight submissions on the same story, and re-checked repeatedly rather than racing to merge. PR #2051 ('US Charges Atlanta Activist for Using GrapheneOS Duress Password to Wipe Phone at Border') was opened before PR #2053 and had chronological priority as the designated surviving candidate if it merged; PR #2054 ('GrapheneOS Defends Its Duress-Wipe Feature After Federal Prosecutors Charge Atlanta Activist Over a Wiped Pixel Phone') is a third independent submission on the same story. Method: (1) initial check via `gh pr view 2051/2053/2054 --json state,mergedAt,closedAt` at the start of this review found all three OPEN and no review file for the story in src/content/reviews/; (2) completed the full independent quality review of #2053 documented above while the other PRs remained unresolved; (3) launched a bounded (10-minute) background poll re-checking `gh pr view 2051 --json state,mergedAt` on a ~20s interval; (4) the poll observed PR #2051 transition to MERGED at 2026-07-27T12:52:35Z (merge commit 685c6dbb9), with its own Chief Editor review recorded in commit 84ddb80e0 (verdict APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS). Per the explicit duplicate-coverage rule, PR #2051 merging makes REJECT mandatory for #2053 regardless of #2053's own quality. PR #2054 remains open and is unaffected by this review; it is not this reviewer's PR to act on.
